trick: Check the three properties one at a time and never assume. Reflexive needs (a,a) for EVERY a; symmetric needs the reverse of every pair present; transitive needs the shortcut of every chain. A relation can be symmetric and transitive and still fail to be reflexive, which is where most marks are lost.

video.query: relations reflexive symmetric transitive equivalence functions class 12 maths

data.prompt: On the set A = {1, 2, 3}, mark each statement true or false.

items.why: It is reflexive, and symmetric and transitive hold vacuously since there are no other pairs to check.
It is symmetric, but (1,1), (2,2) and (3,3) are all missing, so it fails reflexivity — the classic trap.
It contains (1,2) and (2,3) but not (1,3), so the chain has no shortcut.

items.statement: A function f: A → A given by f = {(1,2), (2,3), (3,1)} is a bijection.
items.why: Every element has exactly one image and every element is an image exactly once — one-one and onto.

items.statement: If f: A → B is one-one and A has more elements than B, f can still exist.
items.why: A one-one function needs a distinct image for each element, which is impossible if the codomain is smaller.

trick: Answer inside the principal range or the answer is wrong, however right the angle looks. sin⁻¹ lives in [−π/2, π/2], cos⁻¹ in [0, π], tan⁻¹ in (−π/2, π/2). So cos⁻¹(−½) is 2π/3, not −π/3 — the range for cos⁻¹ never goes negative.

video.query: inverse trigonometric functions principal value branch class 12 maths

data.prompt: Find a principal value, checking the range at every step.

steps.ask: What is the principal range of sin⁻¹?
steps.why: sin⁻¹ takes values in [−π/2, π/2], closed at both ends.
Both 7π/6 and 11π/6 have sine −1/2, but only −π/6 lies in the principal range.

steps.ask: What is the principal range of cos⁻¹?
steps.why: cos⁻¹ takes values in [0, π] — never negative, which is the point most often missed.
cos(2π/3) = −1/2 and 2π/3 lies in [0, π]. −π/3 is outside the range and its cosine is +1/2 anyway.
−π/6 + 2π/3 = −π/6 + 4π/6 = 3π/6 = π/2. This is the identity sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 at work.

data.answer: π/2 — as sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 guarantees for every x in [−1, 1].

trick: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: AB and BA are usually different and may not both exist. For AB to exist, the columns of A must equal the rows of B, and the answer has the rows of A and the columns of B. Check that shape rule before doing any arithmetic.

video.query: matrix multiplication transpose symmetric skew symmetric class 12 maths

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about matrices.

items.statement: If A is 2×3 and B is 3×4, then AB is 2×4.
items.why: Inner dimensions match (3 = 3), and the product takes the outer ones.

items.statement: With A 2×3 and B 3×4, BA also exists.
items.why: BA would need the columns of B (4) to equal the rows of A (2). They do not, so BA is undefined.

items.statement: For a skew-symmetric matrix, every diagonal element is zero.

items.why: The order reverses: (AB)' = B'A'. This reversal is worth a mark on its own.

items.statement: Every square matrix can be written as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix.
items.why: A = ½(A + A') + ½(A − A'), the first symmetric and the second skew-symmetric.

items.statement: If AB = 0 then either A = 0 or B = 0.
items.why: Unlike numbers, two non-zero matrices can multiply to the zero matrix.

trick: The sign pattern of the cofactors alternates + − + along the top row, and a dropped minus sign is the commonest way a correct method produces a wrong answer. When |A| = 0 the system is not automatically inconsistent — check (adj A)B: if it is zero the system has infinitely many solutions, otherwise none.

video.query: determinants cofactor adjoint inverse consistency of system class 12 maths

data.prompt: Expand a determinant, watching every sign.
data.problem: Evaluate |A| where A = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 10]], expanding along the first row.

steps.ask: What is the sign pattern along the first row?
steps.why: The cofactor sign is (−1)^(i+j), giving + − + across the first row.

steps.ask: What is the minor of the element 1?
steps.why: Delete row 1 and column 1, leaving [[5,6],[8,10]], whose determinant is 50 − 48 = 2.

steps.ask: What is the contribution of the element 2, with its sign?
steps.why: The minor is [[4,6],[7,10]] = 40 − 42 = −2, and the cofactor sign is minus, so the term is −2 × (−2) = +4.
1(2) − 2(−2) + 3(32 − 35) = 2 + 4 − 9 = −3. Losing the sign on the middle term would give +5 instead.

data.answer: |A| = −3, so A is invertible and the corresponding system has a unique solution.

trick: Differentiable implies continuous, but never the reverse — |x| at x = 0 is the counterexample to keep in your pocket. To test continuity at a point, check three things: the left limit, the right limit and the value of the function, and all three must agree.

video.query: continuity differentiability chain rule class 12 maths

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about continuity and differentiability.

items.why: Differentiability at a point requires the limit of the difference quotient to exist, which forces continuity there.
f(x) = |x| is continuous everywhere but has no derivative at 0 — the left and right derivatives are −1 and +1.

items.statement: A function continuous at x = a must satisfy lim(x→a⁻)f(x) = lim(x→a⁺)f(x) = f(a).
items.why: All three must exist and be equal; a jump or a hole breaks one of them.
It is not even defined at 0, so continuity cannot hold there — though it is continuous on its own domain.

items.statement: The derivative of a constant function is 1.
items.why: It is 0. A constant does not change, so its rate of change is zero.

trick: f'(x) = 0 finds the candidates, not the answer — the second derivative decides which is which. f''> 0 means minimum, f'' < 0 means maximum, and if f'' = 0 the test says nothing and you must look at the sign change of f'. Remember which way round it goes: a positive second derivative bends the curve upwards, which is a valley.

video.query: maxima minima second derivative test increasing decreasing class 12 maths

data.prompt: Find and classify the turning points.

steps.why: Differentiate term by term: 3x², −12x, +9, and the constant vanishes.
Differentiate f'(x) = 3x² − 12x + 9.

steps.ask: At x = 1, f'' = −6. What does that mean?
steps.why: A negative second derivative means the curve is concave down — a peak, so x = 1 is a local maximum.

steps.ask: At x = 3, f'' = +6. What does that mean?
steps.why: Positive second derivative, concave up, a valley — x = 3 is a local minimum.

data.answer: Local maximum at x = 1 with f(1) = 5; local minimum at x = 3 with f(3) = 1.

trick: Independent and mutually exclusive are opposites, not synonyms. Mutually exclusive means they cannot both happen, so P(A∩B) = 0; independent means one tells you nothing about the other, so P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B). Two events with non-zero probability can never be both.

video.query: conditional probability independent mutually exclusive bayes theorem class 12

data.prompt: A Bayes' theorem problem, one step at a time.
data.problem: Bag I holds 3 red and 4 black balls; Bag II holds 5 red and 6 black. A bag is chosen at random and one ball drawn. It is red. What is the probability it came from Bag I?

steps.why: The bag is chosen at random from two bags, so each has probability 1/2.
Bag I has 3 red out of 7 balls.
Bag II has 5 red out of 11 balls.

steps.ask: What is the total probability of drawing red?

steps.why: Bayes: (3/14) ÷ (34/77) = 33/68. Note it is below ½, because Bag I has the lower share of red balls.

trick: Variance is the square of the standard deviation, so the standard deviation carries the same unit as the data and the variance does not. Adding a constant to every observation leaves both unchanged; multiplying every observation by k multiplies the standard deviation by |k| and the variance by k².

video.query: mean variance standard deviation coefficient of variation class 12 maths

data.prompt: Compute a variance, then see what happens when the data are transformed.

steps.why: The total is 40 over 8 observations, so the mean is 5.

steps.ask: What is the sum of the squared deviations from the mean?

steps.why: It is the positive square root of the variance: √4 = 2.

steps.ask: If 3 is added to every observation, the new standard deviation is?
steps.why: Adding a constant shifts every value and the mean equally, so the spread is untouched. It stays 2.

steps.ask: If instead every observation is doubled, the new variance is?
steps.why: Standard deviation doubles to 4, so the variance becomes 4² = 16 — it multiplies by k², not by k.

data.answer: Mean 5, variance 4, standard deviation 2. Adding 3 changes nothing; doubling gives sd 4 and variance 16.
